summary:
RegiÃ³n de Antofagasta stands under Chile's national legal framework, which the dedicated country dossier (Outright International, published 12 March 2026) sets out in full and against which it records no Antofagasta-specific legal, incident or enforcement finding and no division-level information. A trans visitor to the region therefore faces the national rules: same-sex marriage and joint adoption legal since March 2022; the criminal code's treatment of sexual orientation and gender identity as aggravating circumstances in hate-motivated offences since 2012; legal gender recognition on a self-determination basis since 2019, with no medical or surgical conditions attached; and a third sex option on birth certificates for intersex children since 2006.

Documented abuse in the region is rising faster than the national average. Movilh's XXIV Annual Human Rights Report (HECHOS 2025), published in March 2026, places Antofagasta at 2.09% of nationally documented abuse cases, a year-on-year rise of 45.45% in 2025 and the second-largest regional increase recorded, behind one region that grew by 150%. Across Chile the report counts 3,620 cases and complaints of discrimination in 2025, an increase of 27.1% and the highest annual figure in 24 years.

Antofagasta is part of a general national pattern rather than an exception. Of the 16 regions Movilh tracks, 14 recorded increases in 2025 and only ValparaÃ­so (-17.56%) and Metropolitana (-14.35%) recorded falls. Movilh reads the shift as hatred expanding into regions where public debate is less visible, which makes a moderate regional share an indicator of documented harm diffusing outward rather than evidence of a quieter local environment.

The policy environment has also moved backwards at national level. In the 2025-26 rollback, the Chilean congress excluded the Gender Identity Support Program (PAIG) from the 2026 budget bill, an action condemned by civil society groups and by Chile's national ombudsman for children.
tangentialFactors:
National protections operate as the ceiling for a visitor in Antofagasta, and the absence of region-specific findings means they cannot be assumed to be implemented locally with any particular rigour. The Outright International dossier carries no Antofagasta data on detention practice, policing, health access or local facilities, so the region-specific picture rests on Movilh's abuse statistics rather than on any local enforcement record.

Movilh's 2025 figures show the deterioration is distributed nationally. Only two of 16 regions fell, and the two that rose most sharply include one region at +150% alongside Antofagasta at +45.45%, against a national increase of 27.1%. A visitor comparing Antofagasta with the capital region would see the opposite direction of travel to what the raw share alone suggests, since Metropolitana declined while Antofagasta grew.

The exclusion of the Gender Identity Support Program from the 2026 budget sits in the same period as the rising abuse figures, and civil society groups and the national ombudsman for children both condemned it. Whether the program's withdrawal altered care access in Antofagasta is not established by the available sources.
localsOnly:
Residents of Antofagasta live under the same national rights regime as elsewhere in Chile, including gender recognition by self-determination since 2019, the 2012 hate-crime provisions and the third sex option on birth certificates since 2006. What differs locally is the documented direction of abuse: Antofagasta's share of nationally recorded cases rose to 2.09% in 2025, up 45.45% year on year, the second-fastest regional growth Movilh records.

The 2025 national total of 3,620 cases and complaints of discrimination is the highest in 24 years, and residents of the region are part of the 14 regions that rose rather than the two that fell. Movilh attributes the pattern to the spread of hatred into regions with less public debate, which has direct consequences for the visibility of local reporting and for the political pressure available to secure services.

Locals also bear the effects of the national policy reversal. The Gender Identity Support Program was dropped from the 2026 budget bill by congress, and the decision drew formal condemnation from civil society organisations and from the national ombudsman for children.
outOfScopeNotes:
The 2024 Antofagasta share of nationally documented abuse cases is not reproduced in Movilh's 2025 edition, so the base from which the 45.45% rise was calculated cannot be verified from the source supplied here; the growth figure itself is stated directly by the report.

No source in this inventory documents Antofagasta-specific incidents, police conduct, court outcomes, detention conditions, healthcare or shelter provision, or any local implementation of the national gender-recognition and hate-crime rules. Those questions remain unresolved rather than negative: the Outright International dossier's silence on the region reflects the scope of its national report, not an assessment that local conditions are sound.

The practical effect of the Gender Identity Support Program's exclusion from the 2026 budget on service delivery in Antofagasta is not sourced, and no local or national figure quantifying the loss of support was available at the time of writing.
